lesson.title: What makes an element?

lead.text: Open the carbon atom and you find that most of it is empty space. Near the middle sits a tiny, dense lump called the nucleus, and nearly all of the atom's weight is packed into it. Around the nucleus, far out by comparison, are much lighter particles. If the nucleus were a pea in the middle of a football pitch, those outer particles would be out near the stands.

Chemists have found that an atom holds three kinds of particle in all. Two kinds are packed together in the nucleus and the third kind lives outside it. The picture compares the nucleus with the whole atom. The next screen names each kind of particle.

afterFigure.text: Switch between the two views. The first shows size, with the nucleus as a pea on a pitch. The drawing is only roughly to scale, since at true scale the nucleus would be too small to see. The second shows weight: nearly all of the atom sits in the nucleus, and the particles outside add a sliver. The rest of this lesson is about counting what the atom holds, starting with the nucleus.

lead.text: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. A proton carries a small positive electric charge, which we write as +1. A neutron carries no charge at all. The particles outside the nucleus are electrons, and each one carries a negative charge of −1. Electrons are far lighter than the other two. It takes nearly two thousand of them to weigh as much as one proton.
Opposite charges pull on each other, and that pull keeps the electrons around the nucleus. The charges also give us something to count, which is how we will tell atoms apart.

afterFigure.text: Look at the nucleus of each atom in the picture. It holds protons and neutrons together, and the electrons are all outside it. So when we count the particles in a nucleus we add the protons to the neutrons and leave the electrons out. The carbon atom here has six protons and six neutrons, which makes twelve particles in its nucleus. The lithium atom has three protons and four neutrons, which makes seven.

steps.headline: The count that names an atom

lead.text: Now we can ask what makes carbon carbon. Put the carbon atom next to an oxygen atom and a lithium atom, and count the particles of each kind. All three counts differ from one atom to the next, so the task is to find which count goes with the name. Carbon has six protons, oxygen has eight and lithium has three.

Every carbon atom ever found has exactly six protons, and every atom with six protons is carbon. Add one proton to a carbon nucleus and you have nitrogen, a different substance with different behaviour. The number of protons is what names the atom.

afterFigure.text: This count has its own name, the atomic number, written Z. Carbon has Z = 6, oxygen has Z = 8 and lithium has Z = 3. An element is a substance made only of atoms with the same atomic number. Chemists list the elements in order of Z, and that list is the periodic table. To turn carbon into any other element you would have to change the number of protons in its nucleus, and the next screens test whether changing anything else could do it.

lead.text: The last screen named one count as the atomic number. Here an atom is described by two of its counts, and only one of them is the one you need.

steps.headline: Changing a neutron or an electron

lead.text: Take the carbon atom and add one neutron to its nucleus. The nucleus now holds seven neutrons and six protons. A neutron has weight but no charge, so the atom is heavier and carries the same charge as before. It still has six protons, so it is still carbon. Atoms like this exist, and a later lesson looks at them closely.

Now change an electron instead. Take one away, and the atom is left with a positive charge, since an electron was carrying −1 and is gone. Add one and the atom becomes negative. An atom that has gained or lost electrons in this way is called an ion. The nucleus has not been touched, so a carbon atom that has lost an electron is still carbon.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both changes. Compare each atom with the plain carbon atom before it. The proton count is six every time, and what differs is the weight or the charge. So the proton count names the element, while the neutron count changes the weight and the electron count changes the charge.

lead.text: Two carbon atoms sit side by side and they are not quite identical. Think about which particle count would have to differ to make one of them a different element.

steps.headline: Why a neutral atom has equal counts

lead.text: Something about the carbon atoms so far deserves a closer look. Each one has six protons and six electrons. That is no accident. Every proton adds +1 to the atom and every electron adds −1, so equal numbers cancel exactly and leave no overall charge. An atom with no overall charge is called neutral, and most atoms in everyday matter are neutral.

This gives a quick way to find one count from another. If an atom is neutral, its electron count equals its proton count. A neutral atom with five electrons has five protons, so its atomic number is 5.

afterFigure.text: Sodium shows the idea with larger numbers. A neutral sodium atom has 11 protons, which add up to +11, and 11 electrons, which add up to −11. The total is zero. Take one electron away and the total becomes +11 − 10 = +1, so the atom is now an ion with a charge of +1. The nucleus is the same in both pictures, and so is the element.

steps.headline: How many electrons does a neutral lithium atom have? Its atomic number is 3.

workedSteps.text: Atomic number 3 means 3 protons. Each carries +1.
A neutral atom has no overall charge, so the electrons must cancel that.
Each electron carries −1, so it takes 3 of them.

steps.headline: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?

workedSteps.text: Count the electrons that cancel it.

lead.text: This atom comes with a neutron count and an electron count. Only one of them leads you to the atomic number, and you need the idea from the last screen to see which.
Aluminium has atomic number 13. Atoms of aluminium commonly lose three electrons and become ions.

lesson.orientation: Use protons to identify an element and separate identity from mass and charge.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Take a pencil and look at the grey tip. The grey stuff is graphite, a form of carbon, and every line you draw leaves a smear of tiny flakes on the paper. Pick one flake and imagine cutting it in half, then cutting one half in half again. You can't really do it, but suppose you could keep going until the piece was too small to see and then too small to cut.

At the end you would be holding a single atom of carbon. Hundreds of thousands of them fit side by side across the width of a human hair, and each one is built from smaller pieces. Those pieces decide what the atom is, how heavy it is and how it behaves when it meets other atoms.

This lesson goes down into one carbon atom and looks at what it is made of. Then we change one piece at a time and ask whether the atom is still carbon. The answers show what makes carbon carbon, and what makes any other kind of atom what it is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell what an atom is from the particles inside it, and say which changes would turn it into something else.
intro.whyItMatters: Every other idea in chemistry starts from what an atom is made of.

recap.keyIdea: An element is set by its number of protons, the atomic number. Neutrons change an atom's weight and electrons change its charge, but neither changes the element.

blocks.text: Back at the pencil, the graphite flake was made of carbon atoms that each have six protons. You saw that one more neutron gives a heavier carbon atom and one electron fewer gives a charged one, and that carbon stays carbon through both. You also found that a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, and that a nucleus holds protons and neutrons only.

recap.nextHook: Two carbon atoms can hold different numbers of neutrons, so they do not weigh the same. The next lesson weighs atoms and works out how many neutrons hide in a nucleus.

questions.prompt: Oxygen has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: Choose the particle that identifies the element.
Z counts protons; it ignores neutrons and electrons.
Which supplied count is the definition of atomic number?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Atomic number counts protons, so Z = 8.

questions.onCorrect: 8. The atomic number is the proton count, whatever the neutrons and electrons are doing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the neutrons. The atomic number counts one kind of particle only.

questions.prompt: One carbon atom has 6 neutrons and another has 7. Why are both of them carbon?
hints: Which particle count names an element?
Compare the proton counts of the two atoms.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each nucleus still contains six protons.

questions.onCorrect: Same proton count, same element. The extra neutron changes the mass, not the identity.

misconceptions.feedback: The masses differ here: one has an extra neutron. Look for the count that stays fixed.
The totals differ, because one nucleus has an extra neutron. Look for what stays fixed.

questions.prompt: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 protons. How many electrons does it have?
hints: Neutral means no net electric charge.
Each proton is +1 and each electron is −1.
How many negative charges cancel the nucleus's positive charge?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Seven electrons cancel the charge of seven protons.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Seven electrons cancel the charge of seven protons, so a neutral atom has equal counts.

misconceptions.feedback: Neutral means the charges cancel, not that there are no electrons.
That adds the neutrons. Neutrons carry no charge, so they play no part in cancelling.

questions.prompt: Aluminium has atomic number 13. How many protons does an aluminium ion contain?
hints: An ion retains its element's nucleus.
Ion formation changes electrons, not the atomic number.
Read the stated atomic number without adjusting it for ion charge.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ion formation changes electrons, so its thirteen protons remain.

questions.onCorrect: 13. Forming an ion changes the electrons only, so the proton count stays the atomic number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the electron count of the ion. The nucleus keeps its own protons.
Check what the question gives you: the atomic number is the proton count.
That is the atom's mass number. Protons are counted alone.

questions.prompt: Which change makes a carbon atom an atom of a different element?
hints: Distinguish identity from charge and mass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the proton count changes the atomic number.

questions.onCorrect: Adding a proton changes the atomic number, so it makes a different element.

misconceptions.feedback: A neutron changes the mass, not the element: the proton count is the same.
Losing an electron makes an ion of carbon. The nucleus, and the element, are the same.

questions.prompt: A fluorine nucleus contains 9 protons and 10 neutrons. How many particles are in its nucleus?
hints: Which particles are inside the nucleus?
Leave the electrons out of the count.
Add the protons to the neutrons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus: 9 + 10 = 19.

questions.onCorrect: 19. The nucleus holds protons and neutrons only. Electrons are outside it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the protons alone. The neutrons are in the nucleus too.
That counts the neutrons alone. The protons are in the nucleus too.

questions.prompt: Which number is the same in both carbon atoms, A and B?
hints: Put A and B side by side. Which counts match?
A and B have different neutron counts, so that cannot be the shared number.
Look at the counts that match, and check that C's differs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both have 6 protons and 6 electrons. Atom C has 7, so the shared number is 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Neutrons can differ and the atom is still carbon. The count that matches is the proton count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the neutron count of B. A has a different one, and both are carbon.
Those are totals. A and B have different totals, yet both are carbon.

questions.prompt: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: Which particle count is the atomic number?
Neutrons are not counted.
Read the proton count straight off the question.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Atomic number is the proton count: 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The atomic number is the proton count and nothing else.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the neutron count. The atomic number is the number of protons.
That adds the neutrons to the protons. The atomic number is protons alone.

questions.prompt: Why must a neutral atom have as many electrons as protons?

acceptedIdeas: Each electron's negative charge cancels one proton's positive charge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal numbers of +1 and −1 charges cancel exactly.

choices.label: Each electron's negative charge cancels one proton's positive charge
Electrons and protons have the same mass
The neutrons carry the leftover charge

questions.onCorrect: Right: equal numbers of positive and negative charges leave no net charge.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass does not matter here. This is about electric charge.
Neutrons carry no charge, so they cannot hold any leftover.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom has 9 electrons and 10 neutrons. What is its atomic number?
hints: What does neutral tell you about electrons and protons?
The atomic number is the proton count.
Ignore the neutrons and match the electrons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Neutral means 9 protons to match 9 electrons, so Z = 9.

questions.onCorrect: 9. Neutral means protons equal electrons, and the atomic number is the proton count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the neutron count. It has no effect on the atomic number.
That adds the neutrons. The atomic number is protons alone.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom has 14 electrons and 16 neutrons. How many particles are in its nucleus?
hints: How many protons does a neutral atom with 14 electrons have?
The nucleus holds protons and neutrons.
Add the protons to the neutrons.
questions.onCorrect: 30. Neutral gives 14 protons, and the nucleus holds protons plus neutrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts neutrons only. The protons are in the nucleus too.
That includes the electrons, which are outside the nucleus.
That counts protons only. The neutrons are in the nucleus too.
